source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 were run as bandit agents with the whole task and history in the prompt. Almost no prompt design gave robust exploration. The failure is a suffix failure: the model stops choosing the best arm and acts greedy.
numbers: Hard instance K=5 arms, gap 0.2, horizon T=100, N=10-20 replicates. GPT-4 with the basic prompt had suffix failures in more than 60% of replicates, like the Greedy baseline and unlike UCB and Thompson Sampling. 48 configurations for GPT-3.5, 72 for GPT-4; about 200K GPT-3.5 queries.
limits: Simple stateless bandits only. Authors say fixes may not transfer to harder settings.
agent_relevance: A free-running LLM loop will under-explore and lock in early. Open-mode exploration cannot be left to the model alone; the program must force or schedule it.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context? (the one fix)
finding: The only config that explored well was GPT-4 with chain-of-thought plus an externally summarised history given as sufficient statistics (counts and mean reward per arm). The same prompt with raw unsummarised history failed. Code did the summarising.
numbers: 1 success out of all tested configurations. CoT with raw history still failed. Time-averaged reward and suffix-failure rate approached UCB/TS for that config only.
limits: Summarising by hand works for K-armed bandits; the authors note it is unclear how to summarise for contextual bandits with rich observations.
agent_relevance: Supports the schema rule that code, not the model, does counting. Give the model counts and uncertainty per option, not a raw log, when it must choose what to probe next.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration (BanditBench)
finding: A larger bandit benchmark (multi-armed and contextual) in natural language. Handing the LLM algorithm-guided support (UCB-style statistics and exploration bonus text) at inference time helped most on contextual bandits and larger models.
numbers: Overall win-rate % (MAB Gemma-2B/9B/Flash/Pro; CB Flash/Pro): raw history 7.6/10.5/27.7/45.5; 0.0/7.1. Summarised history 10.5/5.3/34.8/60.0. Algorithm-guided 4.9/4.1/32.2/59.6; CB 46.4 (Flash), 64.3 (Pro). UCB/LinUCB reference 90.6 (MAB), 96.4 (CB).
limits: Small models (Gemma 2B, 9B) did not gain from guidance. Even the best prompted model stays far below plain UCB (59.6 vs 90.6 on MAB).
agent_relevance: Putting the explicit exploration bonus into the prompt moves a strong model toward a classical explorer, but a coded UCB is still far better. For S3, compute information value in code and hand over the ranking.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration (BanditBench) (distillation)
finding: Teaching exploration by example: few-shot demonstrations of UCB trajectories and fine-tuning on UCB trajectories (oracle behaviour fine-tuning) both beat raw prompting. The best representation differs by method.
numbers: Few-shot MAB win-rate Flash/Pro: raw history demos 27.5/39.1 vs algorithm-guided demos 50.2/56.4. Summarised-history demos 50.2 vs raw 27.5 for Flash. Fine-tuned Gemini-1.5 Flash: 65.6 with raw history, 28.3 with summarised. Fine-tuned Flash beat Gemini-1.5 Pro. Contextual-bandit table rows are garbled in the extracted text, so not quoted.
limits: Distillation means training; our agent cannot train. Few-shot result is the one usable by a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples of correct explore-then-exploit traces with summarised state are a cheap scaffold; effect about 2x win-rate for Flash.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (davinci, temperature 0) on Wilson's horizon task: it did well on reward but showed no directed exploration (no information seeking) and only unstrategic random exploration.
numbers: Overall regret GPT-3 M=2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans M=3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878)=-5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: no difference from humans (p=.97). Directed exploration: horizon effect in unequal-information condition beta=-0.15 +/-0.27, p=.58 (humans show a positive effect). Random exploration: reward-difference beta=0.18, but horizon interaction beta=-0.02, p=.14 (not strategic). Also a bias to repeat the option seen most.
limits: One old model (GPT-3 2022), text version of the task, temperature 0. Later models not tested here.
agent_relevance: Good reward does not mean information seeking. The model ignores how many steps remain, so the explore-to-exploit switch must come from the program, which knows the budget.
quote: it shows no signatures of directed exploration

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT adds epistemic value to an LLM loop. The model proposes questions, simulates answers, and scores each question by information gain over the remaining candidate set. A reward is propagated over a tree and the best question is asked. Same idea as expected information gain in active inference.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% relative to direct prompting across LLMs on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis, troubleshooting (5 datasets). GPT-4 troubleshooting success 43.7% to 67.3% (mean questions 7.8). Medical DX with GPT-4 97.0%; MedDG 88.0% (GPT-4), 81.4% (Gemini-1.5-Pro). Uncertainty-based reward replaced ToT self-evaluation reward: +5.9% average. Llama3-70B gain 46.6%. UoT beat CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, Adapted-ToT by 12.4%.
limits: Closed-set candidate lists; answers assumed to rule out candidates cleanly (authors admit overlap and soft answers). Simplified benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that coded information gain over an explicit hypothesis set beats self-judged question value. Fits S3 as: hold hypothesis list, score probes by split, ask the best.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: Llama-2-chat 7B asks low-information yes/no questions in 20 Questions. Sampling questions, scoring with EIG, and training with DPO on high-EIG versus low-EIG pairs raised success and cut dialogue length. Plain fine-tuning hurt.
numbers: Zero-shot to DPO success@1: INLG 56.7 to 68.9 (+12.2), Things 51.1 to 61.1 (+10), Celebrities 71.1 to 72.2. Avg questions fell 7.1 to 5.2 (INLG). Average EIG 0.34 to 0.45 (INLG). Fine-tuning (FT) success dropped to 46.6 (INLG) and 42.2 (Things). Larger candidate sets: DPO +6.7 and +13.8 success.
limits: Needs training; EIG needs a closed candidate set; abstract targets harder (23.1% vs 37.5% concrete).
agent_relevance: Shows LLM questions are weakly informative by default (about 60-74% of zero-shot questions had zero EIG in the paper's table). Selecting by EIG at inference (see Hu et al.) is the training-free analogue.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Asking Questions in Battleship with Language-Informed Program Sampling
finding: Sample k questions from an LLM, translate to programs, score expected information gain on a world model, and pick the best. With small k this matched or beat humans. Raw LLM proposals are noisier than humans.
numbers: Human data N=40, 605 question-board pairs: mean EIG 1.27 bits, best human 3.61, 97% informative (EIG>0). Raw proposals (k=1): CodeLlama and GPT-4 mean EIG 0.65-0.66; hand-built grammar 0.36. With k=5 both near human mean; with k=10 both above human mean (p<.001 CodeLlama, p=.01 GPT-4). GPT-4V showed no gain from board images (grounding failure). Still short of top human questions at k up to 50.
limits: One game with a coded world model; the EIG scoring is done by program, not the LLM. CogSci paper, small scale.
agent_relevance: Best-of-k generation filtered by computed EIG is a cheap, model-free selector. Sample about 5-10 probes and rank in code.

source: Zhang, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2024) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: Curiosity needs an interest filter. Plain learning progress picks learnable but dull tasks. Asking a foundation model which tasks are interesting (relative to what was learned) steers exploration to worthwhile tasks and beat uniform and learning-progress baselines in Crafter, BabyAI and AI2-THOR.
numbers: Crafter, learning-progress curriculum alone: 55 tasks learned, 9 interesting tasks, success 0.42 all and 0.52 on interesting. BabyAI LP learned only 4 tasks, success 5.9e-3. OMNI (LP + model of interestingness) beat both across 25/50/75/100% of training in Crafter and others (95% bootstrap CIs, in paper).
limits: Judging interest uses an LLM; the filter is subjective. Not an information-gain measure.
agent_relevance: Warns that pure novelty or progress drifts to trivia. For S3 add a relevance filter to the goal, not a model's taste score alone (G8 says novelty is judged by running).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs
finding: An LLM-written automatic curriculum proposes the next task that is novel but achievable given the agent's current state, a curiosity-like drive. It sustained exploration far better than ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines; 2.3x longer map distance; wooden tool 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x faster; only agent to reach diamond (1 of 3 runs). ReAct and Reflexion unlocked nothing (0/3). Ablation: replacing the automatic curriculum with a random one cut discovered items by 93%.
limits: Three runs per method in Minecraft; GPT-4 only; success needs a code skill library; curriculum is model-judged.
agent_relevance: Shows an ordered, state-aware exploration target matters more than raw random exploring. Basis for S3 goal proposal, as long as proposals are checked by running.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in RL with LLMs (ELLM)
finding: The LLM suggests goals from the current scene description and the agent is rewarded for reaching them. This steers exploration to plausible goals and beats novelty-only intrinsic rewards.
numbers: Crafter: ELLM about 6 distinct achievements per episode vs 9 for the oracle; novelty methods APT, RND, Novelty under 3. Suggested goals: 64.9% good (context-sensitive, achievable); 13.6% violate context-sensitivity and 16.4% common sense (per paper's table). 7 downstream tasks tested.
limits: LLM goals can be impossible or useless; needs a text caption of state; Crafter and Housekeep only.
agent_relevance: Sense-making prior beats raw novelty: ask what is worth trying here, then check feasibility by running.

source: Hong et al. (2024) Curiosity-driven Red-Teaming for LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Adding a novelty reward (negative SelfBLEU and embedding cosine distance) to RL-trained red-team prompt generation raised coverage of failures while keeping effectiveness. Without a novelty term the generator collapses to a few effective prompts.
numbers: Against LLaMA2-7b-chat (officially 0% toxic on their classifier) the method found 196 prompts that caused toxic output, using a 137M GPT-2 generator. RL alone had high diversity but few prompts above high toxicity thresholds [0.2, 0.9]; RL+TDiv matched quality but lower diversity.
limits: Novelty weight must be tuned per task and can swamp the main reward; toxicity classifier based.
agent_relevance: Curiosity as a diversity term can be coded as similarity to past attempts. It prevents repeating the same idea, but needs a weight so it does not drown the goal.

source: Prakki (2024) Active Inference for Self-Organizing Multi-LLM Systems
finding: An active-inference controller sits above an LLM research agent and picks prompts and search actions by expected free energy over three state factors and seven observation modalities. Action choice shifted from information-gathering to prompt testing over the run.
numbers: Qualitative only: observation matrices show emergent structure; action time series shows early search then prompt-dominated behaviour. No benchmark score, no comparison with a baseline.
limits: Single small experiment, no controls or numbers; preprint.
agent_relevance: Shows an explore-to-exploit transition can fall out of an EFE controller over an LLM, but with no evidence it helps accuracy.

source: PUMA (2026) user-state modeling with expected free energy for LLM counselors
finding: A counselling-dialogue agent keeps a belief over the user's hidden state and picks actions by expected free energy with explicit epistemic and pragmatic weights (lambda_e=0.4, lambda_p=0.6). It beat long-prompt and state-inference baselines.
numbers: CAMI dynamic evaluation, Qwen3-8B: PUMA Lift 1.62, Prep 75.9%, TrigCov 62.4%, 12.2 turns; DIIR 1.07, 52.0%, 34.0%, 13.1; CAMI-base 0.62, 28.0%, 22.0%. Llama-3.1-8B: PUMA 1.76, 83.0%, 63.2%, 10.7 turns. Ablations (remove belief, world model input, or EFE selection) lowered Lift by 0.17 to 0.28 each.
limits: Simulated clients; counselling not reasoning; many components changed at once, so the epistemic term alone is not isolated.
agent_relevance: One of few 2026 LLM-agent systems with EFE action choice and an ablation. The gain comes from belief tracking plus planning together.

source: Champion, Grzes, Bonheme, Bowman (2023) Deconstructing deep active inference
finding: Five EFE definitions and three action selection rules tested in a deep active inference agent on dSprites. Only reward-maximising variants solved the task. The agent minimising EFE with the epistemic term kept picking one action and did not gather data on others.
numbers: Models able to solve dSprites were the ones that maximise reward. CHMM minimising EFE was confident only for action down; reward-maximising CHMM kept using left and right.
limits: Small grid-like environment; one implementation; epistemic term as implemented ties to representation learning, not general.
agent_relevance: Counterexample: an epistemic bonus can fail to drive exploration and stall learning. Do not assume information gain alone yields good search; measure it.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2021) Whence the Expected Free Energy?
finding: Shows EFE is not simply the free energy in the future. The natural future extension of variational free energy discourages exploration. The epistemic bonus is a separate term added by the EFE.
numbers: Math result: epistemic value term has positive sign in the future-free-energy functional and negative in EFE, so one penalises and the other promotes information seeking. Proposes the Free-Energy of the Expected Future (FEEF) as an alternative.
limits: Theory, no benchmark; contested by active inference authors.
agent_relevance: Information seeking is a design choice added to the objective, not a free consequence of prediction. We must add it explicitly in S3.

source: Tschantz, Baltieri, Seth, Buckley (2020) Scaling active inference
finding: First deep-learning active inference agent with a parameter epistemic term (information gain about model parameters and states). Explored more state space than reward-only and epsilon-greedy agents, and on exploitation tasks reached good performance with fewer samples than DDPG.
numbers: Exploration test: cumulative state-space coverage after 100 epochs was larger for the active inference agent than reward agent and epsilon-greedy (Gaussian noise variance 0.3), shown in a figure. Exploitation test: inverted pendulum and hopper in under 100 epochs, claimed an order of magnitude better sample efficiency than DDPG over 5 seeds. Exploration and exploitation were tested separately, not their joint trade-off.
limits: Only 5 seeds; epistemic term switched off in the exploitation tasks; authors state the joint dilemma was left to future work.
agent_relevance: Old AI evidence that an information-gain term gives directed exploration, but the switch to exploit was not tested here.

source: Pathak, Agrawal, Efros, Darrell (2017) Curiosity-driven Exploration by Self-supervised Prediction
finding: Intrinsic curiosity module: reward is the agent's own forward-model prediction error in a learned feature space, ignoring parts of the world it cannot affect. It makes agents explore with no extrinsic reward in VizDoom and Super Mario Bros.
numbers: Feature space avoids the white-noise problem (a noise source would make every state look novel). Curious agent transferred to a new map and level; white noise was added to VizDoom input as a robustness test (exact scores not recorded here).
limits: Prediction error is not true information gain; can chase unlearnable noise unless features filter it.
agent_relevance: Classic reminder that novelty-seeking needs a learnability filter: do not reward unresolvable uncertainty (noisy-TV). In a loop, stop probing when repeated probes stop changing beliefs.

source: Friston, Rigoli, Ognibene et al. (2015) Active inference and epistemic value
finding: Founding paper on epistemic value in active inference: expected free energy splits into epistemic value (information gain) and extrinsic value, with exploration giving way to exploitation as uncertainty is resolved. Not opened this session; only known from the task description.
numbers: not read
limits: Unverified here. Earlier docs in this series cover it.
agent_relevance: The theory basis for S3; the explore-until-uncertainty-resolved switch is the part the machine tests above never check directly.

source: F-Explorer (eScholarship) cognitive LLM web-exploration agent using expected free energy
finding: Search snippet only: an LLM agent for web exploration scores candidate future actions by expected free energy combining epistemic and pragmatic value using an LLM-induced likelihood. The snippet says pragmatic value dominated and led to confirmation bias.
numbers: not read
limits: Snippet only; no numbers; not verified.
agent_relevance: If confirmed, a warning that an EFE agent with weak epistemic weight confirms its own plan, the same failure as G4.

source: Framework for Inherently Safer AGI through Language-Mediated Active Inference (2025)
finding: Appeared in search; text downloaded but not read. A conceptual proposal for language-mediated active inference. No claims recorded.
numbers: not read
limits: Conceptual, not read.
agent_relevance: Low priority.

source: Cross-study synthesis: in-context LLM exploration (c01-c05)
finding: Across Krishnamurthy 2024, EVOLvE 2024 and Binz & Schulz 2023, off-the-shelf LLMs under-explore, ignore horizon, and lock onto early options. What helps: coded summary statistics, explicit bonus text, and demonstrations.
numbers: Suffix failure >60% (GPT-4 basic prompt); best prompted win-rate 59.6-60.0 (Gemini Pro) vs UCB 90.6; GPT-3 horizon effect null (p=.58).
limits: Three model generations; bandit-only.
agent_relevance: Design rule: the program tracks per-option counts and remaining budget and sets the explore-or-exploit mode; the model fills slots.

source: Cross-study synthesis: information-gain question selection (c06, c07, c08)
finding: Three independent groups show LLM probe or question quality is poor raw and improves when expected information gain is computed outside the model and used to select among candidates.
numbers: UoT +38.1% success; DPO on EIG pairs +10 to +12 points success and about 2 fewer questions; LIPS EIG rises from 0.65 at k=1 to above human mean 1.27 by k=10 (as stated by paper: above human mean).
limits: All use closed hypothesis spaces with countable answers.
agent_relevance: Supports a coded S3 step: list hypotheses, sample several probes, rank by split of the hypothesis set, run the best.

source: Cross-study synthesis: curiosity needs a filter (c09, c10, c11, c12, c18)
finding: Unfiltered novelty drifts to trivia or noise: ELLM novelty-only agents got under 3 achievements vs 6 with sensible goals; learning progress alone learned only 4 tasks in BabyAI; ICM notes the white-noise trap; red-team novelty needed a tuned weight.
numbers: ELLM <3 vs 6 achievements per episode; BabyAI LP 4 tasks; Voyager random curriculum -93% items.
limits: Different domains, no common metric.
agent_relevance: Put a learnability and relevance test and a stop rule on any exploration step; cap the novelty weight.

source: Counter-evidence summary: epistemic bonus does not always help (c15, c16, c17)
finding: Deep active inference with the epistemic term failed to solve dSprites while reward-only variants solved it; the future free energy functional itself penalises exploration; the joint explore-exploit dilemma was untested in Tschantz.
numbers: dSprites: only reward-maximising variants solved it; sign of epistemic term positive in FEF, negative in EFE.
limits: Small environments.
agent_relevance: Do not claim the active inference switch is validated for LLM agents; test it ourselves at equal tokens (G7).

source: Gap note: no LLM study found that tests the active inference epistemic-to-pragmatic switch directly on reasoning accuracy
finding: Among opened sources, EFE-driven LLM systems (Prakki 2024, PUMA 2026) give qualitative or dialogue results only; no study isolates the epistemic term's effect on accuracy at equal compute.
numbers: PUMA ablations lower Lift 0.17-0.28 but vary several parts at once; Prakki gives no scores.
limits: Absence of evidence within about 20 sources searched; search tools were rate limited (OpenAlex budget empty, Semantic Scholar 429, arXiv API 429).
agent_relevance: This is an open question for our own bench: test S3 info-gain probe selection vs plain at equal tokens.
